name: Independent on Sunday cryptic crossword No 1,712

indicators.note: one thing sitting in another means it is placed inside the second

blocks.note: sly means secretive or furtive
in Nice, a French city, the word for 'here' is 'ici'

explanation.surface: A traveller in Nice muses about a secretive island somewhere in the Mediterranean.
explanation.walkthrough: Nice looks like the adjective meaning pleasant, but it is the French city, so 'Nice here' asks for a French word.
explanation.definitionFit: The largest island in the Mediterranean, lying off the toe of Italy, so it is a straightforward example of the category.

clue.text: Grounds to invest in South America

indicators.note: to put money into something is to place it within, so one part sits inside another

blocks.note: S is the compass abbreviation for south
US, the United States, stands for America
to invest money is to spend it

explanation.surface: Someone weighs up reasons to put their money into South American ventures.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grounds' reads as a noun meaning reasons, but it is a verb, as when a pilot or a teenager is grounded.
explanation.definitionFit: To ground a pilot or a pupil is to bar them from activity for a time, which is to suspend them.

clue.text: Female replaces husband in conglomeration of merchants and artisans

indicators.note: one thing replacing another swaps a letter out for a different one
a conglomeration is a jumbled mass, so the letters are heaped together in a new order

blocks.note: F is the standard abbreviation for female
H is the abbreviation for husband, the letter taken out
taken as written, the letters to work on

explanation.surface: A woman takes her husband's place in a guild bringing together traders and skilled workers.
explanation.walkthrough: Swap the H in MERCHANTS for F to get MERCFANTS, then rearrange those letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Artisans are skilled manual workers who make things by hand, the same people described as craftsmen.

clue.text: Fast or slow having nothing to lose

indicators.note: something lost is no longer there, so letters drop out of the word

blocks.note: lento is the musical direction for a slow tempo
O looks like zero, so it stands for nothing

explanation.surface: A puzzle about whether to go fast or slow when there is nothing at stake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fast' looks like the opposite of slow, but it is a noun: a period of abstinence. LENTO loses its O.
explanation.definitionFit: The forty days before Easter are the Christian season of fasting, so the noun fast describes it.

indicators.note: fifty per cent is half, so only half the word is kept and the rest dropped

blocks.note: voters return a candidate to parliament, that is, elect them
riches are wealth; its first half is kept

explanation.surface: Getting half of one's fortune back would certainly be thrilling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Return' suggests a refund, but in British politics an MP is returned, that is elected. The first three of the six letters of RICHES follow.
explanation.definitionFit: An electric atmosphere or performance is thrilling and charged with tension, a common figurative use.

blocks.note: first meaning: the BBC's weekly magazine of that name, which closed in 1991
second meaning: one who hears, from Latin audire, to hear

explanation.walkthrough: 'Auditor' suggests an accountant checking books, but its root sense is a hearer. The Listener was a BBC weekly magazine, closed in 1991.
explanation.definitionFit: An auditor in the old sense is someone in an audience who hears, and the BBC published a weekly under that name.

blocks.note: first meaning: terms insisted on, as in a contract
second meaning: shapes behaviour by repetition, as in conditioning

explanation.walkthrough: 'Trains' looks like railway carriages; it is the verb, to teach by habit.
explanation.definitionFit: Conditions are stipulations attached to a deal, and to condition an animal is to train its responses.

blocks.note: first meaning: bring up a point for discussion
second meaning: increase, as a salary or a bid
third meaning: bring up children or livestock
fourth meaning: hoist upwards

explanation.surface: Someone proposes improving the lift at the back of a building.
explanation.walkthrough: This is a quadruple definition: four separate words each mean the answer, with 'to' joining them.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb covers proposing a topic, increasing an amount, bringing up young, and hoisting something higher.

indicators.note: something done badly comes out wrong, so the letters end up in the wrong order

blocks.note: taken as written, the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Someone panics on a frozen slope.
explanation.walkthrough: The Cresta Run is a famous ice toboggan run at St Moritz in Switzerland.
explanation.definitionFit: The Cresta is a natural ice track for skeleton tobogganing, so it is an icy run by name.

clue.text: It doesn't pay to upset America endlessly

indicators.note: without ends means both the first and last letters are cut away
to upset is to knock over and disorder, so the letters are thrown into a new arrangement

blocks.note: America with its first and last letters gone

explanation.surface: A warning that endlessly antagonising the USA is a losing game.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition leans on the proverb 'crime doesn't pay'. Trim both ends of AMERICA and rearrange what is left.
explanation.definitionFit: The saying that crime does not pay lets the whole phrase stand in for law-breaking itself.

blocks.note: SP, starting price, is the betting odds at the start of a race
Queen Anne, the first of the pair
R, for Regina, is the abbreviation for a queen

explanation.surface: A card player at the bridge table weighs the odds of holding two queens.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bridge' and 'queens' suggest the card game, but bridge is the definition, something that spans. SP is the bookmakers' starting price; the queens are Anne and R for Regina.
explanation.definitionFit: A spanner is something that spans a gap, which is exactly what a bridge structure does over a river.

indicators.note: building is constructing something new out of materials, so the letters are assembled afresh

blocks.note: taken as written, the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A woman named Dawn takes out cover on some property.
explanation.walkthrough: Dawn looks like a woman's name and 'building' like the insured property; both are doing other jobs.
explanation.definitionFit: Daybreak, when the sun first appears over the horizon, is both dawn and sunrise, a direct synonym.

clue.text: Consumes escalope after turtle soup for starters

indicators.note: starters are what come at the beginning, so each word yields only its opening letter

blocks.note: the opening letters of these four words

explanation.surface: A diner tucks into an escalope following a bowl of turtle soup as the first course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For starters' suggests the soup course; it tells you to take the first letter of each of the four words before it.
explanation.definitionFit: Both verbs describe taking food into the body, so they are interchangeable in a dinner scene.

clue.text: Let bloke from Bow attach architectural feature

indicators.note: a Cockney, born within the sound of Bow bells in London's East End, drops the aitch at the start of words

blocks.note: 'him' refers to a bloke, a man; spoken in Cockney it loses its first letter
a pediment is the triangular gable above a classical portico

explanation.surface: An East End man is allowed to fix a decorative piece onto a building.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Let' reads as allow, but it is the noun meaning a hindrance, as in 'without let or hindrance' or a let in tennis.
explanation.definitionFit: A let is an old legal word for an obstruction, the same sense as an obstacle or hindrance.

blocks.note: steaming is a way of cooking
hips are joints of the body

explanation.surface: A chef prepares cuts of meat in pots and pans.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Joints' and 'vessels' sound like a roast and cooking pots; here they are body parts and ships.
explanation.definitionFit: Ships powered by steam engines are sea vessels, so the general word covers this specific kind.

indicators.note: a thing that cuts into another goes inside it, splitting it in two

blocks.note: the Dee is a river in Scotland and in Wales
the MOT is the annual roadworthiness test on British vehicles

explanation.surface: Someone harvests a cutting from the lower reaches of the River Test, an English chalk stream.
explanation.walkthrough: The River Test is a real Hampshire river, so it wants to be read together; here they are separate, River giving DEE and Test giving MOT.
explanation.definitionFit: To reduce someone to a lower rank or grade is to demote them; lower is used as a verb here.

blocks.note: first meaning: signs again, with a hyphen after the first two letters
second meaning: gives up a post

explanation.surface: A manager agrees a new deal and then promptly quits.
explanation.walkthrough: The same letters read as RE-SIGNS, signing again, and as the ordinary word for quitting.
explanation.definitionFit: A player who renews terms puts their signature on a deal again, while someone leaving a job formally quits it.

blocks.note: surface reading: awkward rivals in the region around Newcastle
setter's reading: at bridge the four players are named by compass points, and the pair facing each other across the table are partners, so two adjacent seats are opponents competing for tricks

explanation.walkthrough: In bridge the players are called North, South, East and West, and tricks are what they win. Tyneside, around Newcastle, is in the matching region of England.
explanation.definitionFit: Tyneside lies in that region of England, and the two bridge seats named for it sit side by side as opponents.

clue.text: Rested, having marked out playing field earlier

indicators.note: coming earlier means placed in front, fixing which part comes first

blocks.note: a rec is a recreation ground, a public playing field
a pitch is marked out with white lines

explanation.surface: A groundsman takes a break after painting the lines on a pitch.
explanation.walkthrough: REC, short for recreation ground, is British for a local park with playing fields.
explanation.definitionFit: To lean back or lie down in a relaxed position is to recline, which is a way of taking rest.

indicators.note: something gone off is spoilt and out of order, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written, the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Grasping legends turns out to be worth the effort.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pays off' looks like a phrasal verb meaning succeeds; 'off' alone is the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Compassionate fellow feeling for another person's situation is both understanding and sympathy.

clue.text: Friends in bars discussed people behind bars

indicators.note: something discussed is talked about, so the answer comes from spoken words

blocks.note: pals found in pubs would be inn mates

explanation.surface: Pub-going pals chat about prisoners.
explanation.walkthrough: The two kinds of bar make the joke: pub counters in the wordplay, prison bars in the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Prisoners are the residents of a jail, held in cells with barred windows, so they are its inmates.

clue.text: Green bananas the beginning of your vitality

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its opening letter, so only that one is taken
bananas is slang for crazy, so the letters go wild and rearrange

blocks.note: taken as written
its opening letter

explanation.surface: Eating unripe bananas is where your get-up-and-go starts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Green bananas' reads as unripe fruit; bananas is the slang signal to rearrange GREEN plus Y.
explanation.definitionFit: Liveliness and physical vigour are both described as vitality or energy, so these are synonyms.

indicators.note: to bottle something is to hold it inside, so the letters are enclosed within the words
in a down clue, going up means reading from bottom to top, backwards

blocks.note: letters running across the two words

explanation.surface: Someone kisses Boris while hiding an inner anguish.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters sit across 'kiSSES BOris' and are read backwards, upwards in this down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: To obsess is to preoccupy the mind constantly and distressingly, a sense close to torment as a verb.

indicators.note: something remarkable is out of the ordinary, so the letters fall out of their usual order

blocks.note: taken as written, the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A market stall offers fruit at a startlingly low price.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Remarkably cheap' reads as a bargain; 'Remarkably' is the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A soft, downy stone fruit, so it is a straightforward example of the general category named.

clue.text: Top wine collection mentioned in book?

indicators.note: something mentioned is spoken of, so the word is heard rather than seen

blocks.note: top means best
a cellar is where a wine collection is kept, and the word is also used for the collection

explanation.surface: A list of the finest wines appears in a book.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that the definition is an example: a book is one kind of thing that sells best.
explanation.definitionFit: A hugely popular book topping the sales charts is the classic instance, though other goods can qualify, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Elegant form of transport on the rise

indicators.note: in a down clue, rising means reading from the bottom up, backwards

blocks.note: trams are street railway vehicles, a form of public transport

explanation.surface: A stylish way of getting around is becoming popular.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On the rise' sounds like growing popularity; in a down clue it means read upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Smartly dressed means neat and stylish, so smart and elegant are close synonyms describing appearance.

blocks.note: taps are labelled C and H, for cold and hot
OP, short for opus, is a work of music

explanation.surface: A plumbing job in which the taps have cracked.
explanation.walkthrough: The taps give their two labels, C for cold and H for hot; OP for opus is how a composer's works are numbered.
explanation.definitionFit: To cut wood into pieces with an axe is to chop it, which splits it apart.

blocks.note: un is the French for a
a do is an informal party

explanation.surface: Someone calls off a celebration in France.
explanation.walkthrough: Do is British slang for a party or social event.
explanation.definitionFit: To reverse or annul an action, as with an editing command, is to undo it, effectively cancelling it.

indicators.note: without ends means the first and last letters are trimmed away

blocks.note: relations is a polite word for sexual intimacy

explanation.surface: The happiness that comes from a closeness that never fades.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Endless intimacy' sounds romantic; it means a word for intimacy with both ends cut.
explanation.definitionFit: Elation is a feeling of great happiness and exhilaration, a direct synonym for joy.

blocks.note: Con is short for Conservative, the Tory party
tact is diplomacy, sensitivity in dealing with others

explanation.surface: The effect a Conservative politician's statecraft has had.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Impact' reads as effect; it is meant physically, a collision.
explanation.definitionFit: When two objects collide, they come into physical contact; impact is the moment of striking.

clue.text: Beach borders start of terribly unproductive land

indicators.note: the start of a word is its opening letter, so only that one is kept
to border something is to lie on either side of it, so one part wraps the other

blocks.note: the seaside is the beach
its opening letter

explanation.surface: A beach edges a dreadfully barren stretch of country.
explanation.walkthrough: Set-aside was the EU scheme paying farmers to take fields out of cultivation, and also names those fields.
explanation.definitionFit: Farmland deliberately left out of production under the subsidy scheme grows no crop, so it is unproductive by design.

clue.text: Schumann's opening surprisingly lofty for piano

indicators.note: an opening is where a word begins, so only its first letter is used
a surprising outcome is unexpected, so the letters come out in an unexpected order

blocks.note: its first letter
taken as written, the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A Schumann piano piece begins with an unexpectedly elevated passage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Piano' looks like the instrument for Schumann's music, but it is the musical direction meaning quietly.
explanation.definitionFit: In musical notation piano is the Italian marking for playing quietly, which is what softly means.
